1. fc köln.sourceSentence: Cologne and Düsseldorf love to tease each other. Beer shows it best: Kölsch is light, and Alt is dark. In a Cologne brewery pub, you never order an Alt. Alt belongs to Düsseldorf. The Cologne brewery Früh once had adverts with the slogan Not a bit of Alt. The funny part is that an agency from Düsseldorf wrote them. The usual story says the fight started in 1288. In that year, the Archbishop of Cologne was beaten at the Battle of Worringen. On 14 August 1288, Düsseldorf received its town rights. The story says this was a thank-you for beating Cologne. Historians say this is a legend, an old story that is not true. People from both towns fought on the same side. The town rights had strategic reasons. The real competition is newer. In 1815 both cities became part of Prussia. In the 19th century, Düsseldorf grew fast with industry. In 1946 the British chose Düsseldorf as the capital of the new state of North Rhine-Westphalia. But Cologne was much older. There were two reasons. About 90 percent of Cologne's city centre was destroyed in the war. And Düsseldorf was close to the factories of the Ruhr. Today the rivalry lives on at carnival, the big street party before Lent. Lent is the time of the year just before Easter. In Cologne people shout Alaaf, and in Düsseldorf they shout Helau. The rivalry lives on in sport too. In football, 1. FC Köln plays against Fortuna Düsseldorf. In ice hockey, Kölner Haie play against Düsseldorfer EG. Most of it is friendly fun. In 2005 a Cologne guidebook about Düsseldorf had only empty pages. The joke was that there is nothing to see there. Cologne Zoo invited people from Düsseldorf to come and see the Cologne monkeys.

lxs_1e34b0309c120731.sourceSentence: Cologne and Düsseldorf love to tease each other. Beer shows it best: Kölsch is light, and Alt is dark. In a Cologne brewery pub, you never order an Alt. Alt belongs to Düsseldorf. The Cologne brewery Früh once had adverts with the slogan Not a bit of Alt. The funny part is that an agency from Düsseldorf wrote them. The usual story says the fight started in 1288. In that year, the Archbishop of Cologne was beaten at the Battle of Worringen. On 14 August 1288, Düsseldorf received its town rights. The story says this was a thank-you for beating Cologne. Historians say this is a legend, an old story that is not true. People from both towns fought on the same side. The town rights had strategic reasons. The real competition is newer. In 1815 both cities became part of Prussia. In the 19th century, Düsseldorf grew fast with industry. In 1946 the British chose Düsseldorf as the capital of the new state of North Rhine-Westphalia. But Cologne was much older. There were two reasons. About 90 percent of Cologne's city centre was destroyed in the war. And Düsseldorf was close to the factories of the Ruhr. Today the rivalry lives on at carnival, the big street party before Lent. Lent is the time of the year just before Easter. In Cologne people shout Alaaf, and in Düsseldorf they shout Helau. The rivalry lives on in sport too. In football, 1. FC Köln plays against Fortuna Düsseldorf. In ice hockey, Kölner Haie play against Düsseldorfer EG. Most of it is friendly fun. In 2005 a Cologne guidebook about Düsseldorf had only empty pages. The joke was that there is nothing to see there. Cologne Zoo invited people from Düsseldorf to come and see the Cologne monkeys.

blk_part_01_k_lsch_the_light_beer_of_col.text: Kölsch is a clear, pale gold beer from Cologne. It usually has 4.4 to 5.2 percent alcohol, so it is light and easy to drink. Its secret is the yeast, a tiny living thing that turns sugar into alcohol. In top-fermented beer, the yeast works at the top, at a warm temperature. Kölsch is top-fermented, and this gives it a soft, fruity taste. Then the brewers store the beer cold, like a lager. Lager is beer made with yeast that works at the bottom, at cold temperatures. Kölsch uses both steps, so it tastes a little like fruit but also fresh.

blk_part_01_k_lsch_the_light_beer_of_col.text: The Second World War almost ended the story. Before the war, Cologne had more than 40 breweries. At the end, only two were left. Later, the brewers wanted to protect their beer. In 1986, 24 brewers signed the Kölsch Konvention. This agreement sets the rules for making Kölsch. Only local breweries can use the name. Since 1997 the European Union has protected the name too. So a brewery in another European Union country cannot sell its beer as Kölsch. Famous names today include Früh, Gaffel, Reissdorf, Päffgen and Sünner.

blk_part_02_altbier_the_dark_beer_of_d_s.text: Düsseldorf is about 40 kilometres north of Cologne, on the Rhine. There, people drink a very different beer. Altbier is dark red-brown, with more taste of malt. Malt is grain that has started to grow and then been dried. It gives beer its colour and a sweet taste. Altbier usually has 4.3 to 5.5 percent alcohol. Alt is the German word for old, but the beer is not old. The name tells you that it is made the old way. Like Kölsch, it is top-fermented, a method older than lager. Then it rests in the cold.

blk_part_03_dortmunder_export_the_worker.text: For a long time, Dortmund had more breweries than any other German city. In 1956 Dortmunder Union made more than 100 million litres of beer. It was the first German brewery to make so much in one year. After the Second World War, Export was the favourite beer in Germany. Then in 1970, Pils took first place. Pils is short for Pilsner. When the mines and steel works closed, Export lost many of the people who drank it. Dortmunder Union closed in 1994. Today the old brands belong to one group. The main names are DAB and Brinkhoff's. Brinkhoff's is named after Fritz Brinkhoff, the first brewmaster of Dortmunder Union.

blk_part_05_glasses_waiters_and_customs_.text: The waiter is a Köbes, and a woman is a Köbine. Köbes is the Cologne form of the name Jakob. A Köbes wears a long blue apron and carries a leather money bag. A Köbes is quick with jokes and sometimes short with guests. But that is part of the show. blk_part_05_glasses_waiters_and_customs_.text: Here is the custom that surprises visitors. When your glass is empty, the Köbes brings a full one without asking. Each time, they draw a pencil line on your beer mat. This continues until you put the beer mat on top of your glass. That is the only clear sign for stop. The system is fast. A busy Köbes serves around 200 guests a day, and nobody waits to order. At the end, you pay for the lines on your beer mat. A tip is not required, but people often round up to the next euro.

1. fc köln.simpleMeaning: the football club of the old city
1. fc köln.contextMeaning: the football club of the old city
1. fc köln.sourceSentence: Cologne and Düsseldorf love to tease each other. Beer shows it best: Kölsch is light, and Alt is dark. In a Cologne brewery pub, you never order an Alt. Alt belongs to Düsseldorf. The Cologne brewery Früh once had adverts with the slogan Not a bit of Alt. The funny part is that an agency from Düsseldorf wrote them. The usual story says the fight started in 1288. In that year, the Archbishop of Cologne was beaten at the Battle of Worringen. On 14 August 1288, Düsseldorf received its town rights. The story says this was a thank-you for beating Cologne. Historians say this is a legend, an old story that is not true. People from both towns fought on the same side. The town rights had strategic reasons. The real competition is newer. In 1815 both cities became part of Prussia. In the 19th century, Düsseldorf grew fast with industry. In 1946 the British chose Düsseldorf as the capital of the new state of North Rhine-Westphalia. But Cologne was much older. There were two reasons. About 90 percent of Cologne's city centre was destroyed in the war. And Düsseldorf was close to the factories of the Ruhr. Today the rivalry lives on at carnival, the big street party before Lent. Lent is the time of the year just before Easter. In Cologne people shout Alaaf, and in Düsseldorf they shout Helau. The rivalry lives on in sport too. In football, 1. FC Köln plays against Fortuna Düsseldorf. In ice hockey, Kölner Haie play against Düsseldorfer EG. Most of it is friendly fun. In 2005 a Cologne guidebook about Düsseldorf had only empty pages. The joke was that there is nothing to see there. Cologne Zoo invited people from Düsseldorf to come and see the Cologne monkeys.
